title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Models with Dictionary Learning
hook: If neurons mean several things at once, can we find cleaner units? A sparse autoencoder pulled 4,000+ single-concept features out of one tiny transformer layer.
key_points: Trains a sparse autoencoder (dictionary learning) to extract features from a one-layer transformer.
Decomposed a single 512-neuron MLP layer into more than 4,000 interpretable features.
The features are far more monosemantic than neurons — each tracks one concept.
Example features fire on DNA sequences, legal language, HTTP requests, and Hebrew text.
content_html: Trenton Bricken, Adly Templeton, Joshua Batson, and colleagues at Anthropic tackle a practical version of the superposition problem: if individual neurons are polysemantic, what are the right units to read? Their answer is dictionary learning. They train a sparse autoencoder on the activations of a one-layer transformer and pull out features that are far more monosemantic than the underlying neurons — a single 512-neuron MLP layer decomposes into more than 4,000 interpretable features, each tracking one concept.
extra_html:
How it works

A sparse autoencoder learns to reconstruct a layer's activations using a much larger set of features, only a few of which are active at any moment. That sparsity pressure encourages each learned feature to correspond to a single, recognizable thing rather than a tangled mix. Applied to one 512-neuron MLP layer, the method recovers over 4,000 features, and inspecting them shows clean concepts — features that respond to DNA sequences, legal language, HTTP requests, or Hebrew text.

Why it matters

This turns the superposition idea into a concrete recipe: instead of squinting at neurons that each do several jobs, you can decompose a layer into a dictionary of features that each do one. Getting cleaner, single-concept units is a big step for mechanistic interpretability, because it makes the model's internal vocabulary something you can actually name and study. It set up the obvious next question — whether the same approach holds up on a real production model.
